title: Boys and men: second declension
subtitle: Lesson 7 · Second declension: -us, -ī, -um, -ōs
intro: So far every noun was feminine and ended in *-a*: *puella*, *fēmina*, *porta*. Today the men and boys of the household arrive, and they use a second set of endings. One slave is *servus*, several are *servī*; as the object he is *servum*, and several are *servōs*. New words: *puer* 'boy', *vir* 'man', *servus* 'slave', *dominus* 'master', *equus* 'horse' and *amīcus* 'friendly, a friend'.

vocab.notes: *puer* drops the usual *-us*, but its other forms are regular: *puerum*, *puerī*, *puerōs*.
*vir* is a grown man (compare English 'virile'). Forms: *virum*, *virī*, *virōs*.
*servus* is the model word for today's endings: *servus*, *servum*, *servī*, *servōs*.
*dominus* is the master of the house; the mistress is *domina*, with the *-a* endings you already know.
As an adjective *amīcus* means 'friendly'; on its own it means 'a friend': *amīcus* (a male friend), *amīca* (a female friend).

grammar.title: Second declension: -us, -ī, -um, -ōs
grammar.body:
Many masculine nouns follow the **second declension**. One subject ends in **-us**, several in **-ī**; one object ends in **-um**, several in **-ōs**: *Servus labōrat* 'The slave works', *Servī labōrant* 'The slaves work', *Dominus servum vocat* 'The master calls the slave', *Dominus servōs vocat* 'The master calls the slaves.'

*puer* and *vir* simply have no *-us* in the subject form; everything else is regular: *puerum*, *puerī*, *puerōs*; *virum*, *virī*, *virōs*.

Adjectives you know take the same endings when they describe a man or boy: *servus bonus*, *equum māgnum*, *virī multī*, *puerōs parvōs*. And the old rule still holds: the ending, not the word order, tells you who does what. *Puer equum videt* and *Equum puer videt* both mean 'The boy sees the horse.'

reading.title: Dominus et servī
reading.la: Mārcus puer est et Sextus vir est. Sextus dominus bonus est; servōs multōs habet. Servī saepe labōrant: aquam portant et viās parant. Mārcus equōs amat. Nunc puer equum māgnum spectat, sed nōn timet. Sextus rīdet et puerum laudat. Ubi servī nōn labōrant, fābulās narrant, et Mārcus semper manet: fābulās longās amat. Servī et Mārcus amīcī sunt.
reading.en: Marcus is a boy and Sextus is a man. Sextus is a good master; he has many slaves. The slaves often work: they carry water and prepare the roads. Marcus loves horses. Now the boy is looking at a big horse, but he is not afraid. Sextus laughs and praises the boy. When the slaves are not working, they tell stories, and Marcus always stays: he loves long stories. The slaves and Marcus are friends.
reading.hint: Find the new endings: subjects *servī*, *amīcī*; objects *servōs*, *equōs*, *equum*, *puerum*. Then spot the old *-ās* in *viās* and *fābulās*.
